0087 | \centerline{\bf\uppercase{A general inversion formula}}
0088 | \centerline{\bf\uppercase{for summatory arithmetic functions}}
0089 | \centerline{\bf\uppercase{and its application to the summatory function}}
0090 | \centerline{\bf\uppercase{of the M\"obius function}\footnote[1]{
0091 | 2010 {\it Mathematics Subject Classification.} Primary 11M26, 11M06; Secondary 11NXX.\\
0092 | {\it Key words and phrases.} Summatory function, Moebius function, Dirichlet divisor problem, Riemann zeta function, zero-free region, Dirichlet $L$-function, Siegel--Landau zero.}}
0093 | 
0094 | \bigskip
0095 | 
0096 | \bigskip
0097 | 
0098 | \centerline{\small\sc\uppercase{Sergei~Preobrazhenski\u i}}
0099 | 
0100 | \bigskip
0101 | 
0102 | \hbox to \textwidth{\hfil\parbox{0.9\textwidth}{
0103 | \small {\sc Abstract.} We prove an inversion formula for summatory arithmetic functions.
0104 | 
0105 | As an application, we obtain an arithmetic relationship between summatory Piltz divisor functions
0106 | and a sum of the M\"obius function over certain integers, denoted by $M(x,y)$. With this relationship,
0107 | using bounds for the main and remainder terms in the $k$-divisor problems
0108 | we deduce conditional and unconditional results concerning $M(x,y)$
0109 | and the zero-free region of the Riemann zeta-function and Dirichlet $L$-functions.}\hfil}
0110 | 
0111 | \bigskip
0112 | 
0113 | \bigskip
0114 | 
0115 | 
0116 | 
0117 | {\bf 1. Introduction.} Let $d_k(n)=\sum_{n_1\cdots n_k=n}1$,
0118 | so $d(n)=d_2(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n$.
0119 | The M\"obius function is defined by
0120 | \[
0121 | \mu(n)=
0122 | \begin{cases}
0123 | 1&\text{if $n=1$},\\
0124 | 0&\text{if $n$ is not squarefree},\\
0125 | (-1)^{\omega}&\text{if $n$ is squarefree and $n=p_1\dots p_{\omega}$},
0126 | \end{cases}
0127 | \]
0128 | and the summatory function $M(x)$ (the Mertens function) by
0129 | \[
0130 | M(x)\mathrel{{:}{=}}\sum_{n\le x}\mu(n).
0131 | \]
0132 | 
0133 | Among important problems of analytic number theory are those of investigating the distribution of the summatory functions
0134 | $\sum_{n\le x}d_k(n)$ and $M(x)$. In the case $k=2$ the problem for $\sum_{n\le x}d_k(n)$ is called
0135 | the Dirichlet divisor problem and in the general case it is called the $k$-divisor problem or the Piltz problem.
0136 | Both $\sum_{n\le x}d_k(n)$ and $M(x)$ are closely related to the Riemann zeta-function $\zeta(s)$.
0137 | 
0138 | For a positive integer $n$ let $P^{{-}}(n)$ denote the smallest prime divisor of $n$
0139 | and set $P^{{-}}(1)=\infty$.
0140 | For $y\ge2$ and integer $k\ge1$
0141 | let
0142 | \be\label{Preobdkpny}
0143 | d_k'(n,y)=
0144 | \begin{cases}
0145 | \sum_{n_1\cdots n_k=n}1&\text{if $P^{{-}}(n)>y$},\\
0146 | 0&\text{else}.
0147 | \end{cases}
0148 | \ee
0149 | Define $d_1^{\ast}(n,y)=d_1'(n,y)$ and for integer $k\ge2$
0150 | \[
0151 | d_k^{\ast}(n,y)=
0152 | \begin{cases}
0153 | \sum\limits_{\substack{n_1\cdots n_k=n\\ n_1,\cdots,n_k\not\in\{1,n\}}}1&\text{if $P^{{-}}(n)>y$},\\
0154 | 0&\text{else}.
0155 | \end{cases}
0156 | \]
0157 | We also define the modified Mertens function
0158 | \[
0159 | M(x,y)\mathrel{{:}{=}}\sum_{\substack{n\le x\\ P^{{-}}(n)>y\text{ or }P^{{-}}(n/2)>y}}\mu(n).
0160 | \]
0161 | 
0162 | In this article we establish a direct arithmetic relationship between the summatory functions
0163 | $\sum_{n\le x}d_k^{\ast}(n,y)$ and $M(x,y)$
0164 | by means of a general inversion formula for summatory functions.
0165 | \begin{theorem}[Inversion Formula]\label{PreobInversionF} Let
0166 | \[
0167 | F(X)=\sum_{n\le X}\alpha(n)G\left(\frac Xn\right).
0168 | \]
0169 | Then we have
0170 | \[
0171 | G(X)=\sum_{n\le X}\beta(n)F\left(\frac Xn\right),
0172 | \]
0173 | where
0174 | \be\label{Preobbetan}
0175 | \beta(n)=\begin{cases}
0176 | \frac1{\alpha(1)}&\text{if $n=1$},\\
0177 | \frac1{\alpha(1)}&\left(-\frac{\alpha(n)}{\alpha(1)}+\sum\limits_{\substack{n_1n_2=n\\ n_1,n_2\not\in\{1,n\}}}\frac{\alpha(n_1)
0178 | \alpha(n_2)}{(-\alpha(1))^2}+\sum\limits_{\substack{n_1n_2n_3=n\\ n_1,n_2,n_3\not\in\{1,n\}}}\frac{\alpha(n_1)
0179 | \alpha(n_2)\alpha(n_3)}{(-\alpha(1))^3}+\cdots\right)\\
0180 | &\text{if $n>1$}.
0181 | \end{cases}
0182 | \ee
0183 | \end{theorem}
0184 | 
0185 | We apply this formula in the following way: Let
0186 | \[
0187 | U(x)=
0188 | \begin{cases}
0189 | 1&\text{if $1\le x<2$},\\
0190 | 0&\text{if $x\ge2$},
0191 | \end{cases}
0192 | \]
0193 | \[
0194 | \alpha(n,y)=
0195 | \begin{cases}
0196 | 1&\text{if $P^{{-}}(n)>y$},\\
0197 | 0&\text{else}.
0198 | \end{cases}
0199 | \]
0200 | The identity
0201 | \[
0202 | \frac1{\zeta(s)}\prod_{3\le p\le y}\left(1-\frac1{p^s}\right)^{-1}
0203 | \zeta(s)\left(1-\frac1{2^s}\right)\prod_{3\le p\le y}\left(1-\frac1{p^s}\right)
0204 | =1-\frac1{2^s}
0205 | \]
0206 | implies the identity
0207 | for the summatory functions
0208 | \[
0209 | U(X)=\sum_{n\le X}\alpha(n,y)M\left(\frac Xn,y\right),
0210 | \]
0211 | and by the inversion formula (Theorem~\ref{PreobInversionF}) we get our basic arithmetic identity
0212 | relating $M(X,y)$ to the summatory divisor functions $\sum_{n\le x}d_k^{\ast}(n,y)$:
0213 | \be\label{PreobMXyId}
0214 | M(X,y)=\sum_{n\le X}\beta(n,y)U\left(\frac Xn\right)=\beta(\flr{X/2}+1,y)+\beta(\flr{X/2}+2,y)+\cdots+\beta(\flr{X},y),
0215 | \ee
0216 | where, with $\Omega(n)$ standing for the number of prime divisors of $n$ counted according to multiplicity,
0217 | \[
0218 | \beta(n,y)=\sum_{k=1}^{\Omega(n)}{(-1)}^kd_k^{\ast}(n,y).
0219 | \]
0220 | 
0221 | Note that we can take $\frac{\log X}{\log y}$ as the limit
0222 | of the summation over $k$, since $d_k^{\ast}(n,y)=0$ if $k>\min\left(\Omega(n),\frac{\log X}{\log y}\right)$.
0223 | 
0224 | Let the generating Dirichlet series for the arithmetic function $\beta_l(n,y)=\sum_{k=1}^{l}{(-1)}^kd_k^{\ast}(n,y)$
0225 | be denoted by $F_{l,y}(s)$. Since for $d_k'(n,y)$ defined by~\eqref{Preobdkpny}
0226 | \[
0227 | d_k^{\ast}(n,y)=d_k'(n,y)-kd_{k-1}^{\ast}(n,y)-\binom k2 d_{k-2}^{\ast}(n,y)-\cdots-\binom k{k-1} d_1^{\ast}(n,y),
0228 | \]
0229 | then $F_{l,y}(s)$ is represented as the linear combination of $\zeta^k(s)\prod_{p\le y}\left(1-\frac1{p^s}\right)^k$
0230 | with $1\le k\le l$.
0231 | 
0232 | Let $\Delta_{l,y}(x)$ denote the remainder term in the asymptotic formula
0233 | \[
0234 | \sum_{n\le x}\beta_l(n,y)=\res\limits_{s=1}F_{l,y}(s)\frac{x^s}{s}+\Delta_{l,y}(x).
0235 | \]
0236 | 
0237 | \begin{definition}
0238 | Suppose that $c>0$, $\alpha_1>0$ and $\alpha_2$ are real,
0239 | $x\ge2$, $3\le y(x)\le x$.
0240 | 
0241 | A number $l_0=\flr{\frac{\log x}{\log y}}+1$ is called \textbf{the level}
0242 | for $c$, $\alpha_1$, $\alpha_2$, $y$,
0243 | if we have the bounds
0244 | \be\label{Preobresest}
0245 | \left|\res\limits_{s=1}F_{l_0,y}(s)\frac{x^s}{s}\right|
0246 | \ll xe^{-c(\log x)^{\alpha_1}(\log_{(2)}x)^{\alpha_2}}
0247 | \ee
0248 | and
0249 | \be\label{PreobDeltal0yx}
0250 | |\Delta_{l_0,y}(x)|\ll xe^{-c(\log x)^{\alpha_1}(\log_{(2)}x)^{\alpha_2}}.
0251 | \ee
0252 | 
0253 | That is, if $l_0$ is the level, then~\eqref{PreobMXyId} implies that
0254 | \[
0255 | |M(x,y)|\ll xe^{-c(\log x)^{\alpha_1}(\log_{(2)}x)^{\alpha_2}}.
0256 | \]
0257 | \end{definition}
0258 | We remark that if we take
0259 | \[
0260 | y=y_0\asymp\exp\left(c_0(\log x)^{2/5}(\log_{(2)}x)^{1/5}\right),
0261 | \]
0262 | and if $l_0=\flr{\frac{\log x}{\log y}}+1$
0263 | were the level for some $c>0$, $\alpha_1=3/5$, $\alpha_2=-1/5$,
0264 | then we would have the bound
0265 | \be\label{PreobMxyassert}
0266 | M(x,y_0)=O\left(xe^{-c(\log x)^{3/5}(\log_{(2)}x)^{-1/5}}\right).
0267 | \ee
0268 | (The bound~\eqref{PreobDeltal0yx} can be proved using $l_0$-th derivative
0269 | of the generating Dirichlet series as in~\cite{PreobKoukoulo},
0270 | but the residue term in~\eqref{Preobresest} is quite complicated.)
0271 | From~\eqref{PreobMxyassert} one could infer, using methods of Pintz~\cite{PreobPintz1}, \cite{PreobPintz2},
0272 | the best known zero-free region, and then
0273 | the best known error term in the prime number theorem:
0274 | \begin{theorem}\label{PreobZF}
0275 | With the above assumptions, we have $\zeta(s)\ne0$ in the region
0276 | \be\label{zf}
0277 | \sigma>1-\frac{c}{(\log(|t|+3))^{2/3}(\log\log(|t|+3))^{1/3}},
0278 | \ee
0279 | and, in the prime number theorem,
0280 | \be\label{pnt_e3}
0281 | \psi(x)=x+O\left(xe^{-c(\log x)^{3/5}(\log\log x)^{-1/5}}\right)\quad(x\ge30)
0282 | \ee
0283 | {\rm(}the constant $c$ is not necessarily the same one in every place{\rm)}.
0284 | \end{theorem}
0285 | 
0286 | 
0287 | Remarkably, in the problem of bounding $M_{\chi}(x,y)$,
0288 | the sum of the M\"obius function twisted by a Dirichlet character,
0289 | strong estimates for real non-principal characters $\chi$ (using $y=y_0$)
0290 | could be obtained circumventing
0291 | treatment of the Landau--Siegel zero, since there is no logarithmic derivative in the argument.
0292 | (And there is no residue term~\eqref{Preobresest}
0293 | for nonprincipal characters $\chi\bmod q$.)
0294 | 
0295 | The above fact allows us to prove the following result on the Landau--Siegel zero:
0296 | \begin{theorem}\label{PreobZZ}
0297 | Let $\chi$ be a real non-principal primitive character ${}\bmod q$.
0298 | Suppose that $\chi(2)=1$ and $\beta_0$ is the real zero of Dirichlet $L$-function
0299 | $L(s,\chi)$.
0300 | Then we have
0301 | \[
0302 | \beta_0\le1-\frac{c}{\log q},
0303 | \]
0304 | where the constant $c>0$ is effectively computable.
0305 | \end{theorem}
0306 | \setcounter{theorem}{0}
0307 | This theorem is proved in Section~4.
0308 | By considering modifications of the functions $M_{\chi}(x,y)$
0309 | the theorem can be proved for all real non-principal primitive characters ${}\bmod q$,
0310 | not only for those with $\chi(2)=1$.
0311 | 
0312 | \textbf{2. Inversion formula: A simple numerical example.}
0313 | Here we illustrate usage of the inversion formula
0314 | for a particular choice of the functions $F$, $G$ and a small value of $X$.
0315 | 
0316 | The Dirichlet convolution of arithmetic functions $f$, $g$ is defined by $f*g(n)=\sum_{ab=n}f(a)g(b)$.
0317 | \begin{lemma}[Mertens]\label{PreobMertensLem}
0318 | \[
0319 | \Delta(X)=\psi(X)-\flr{X}
0320 | =\sum_{n\le X}(\log n-d(n))M\left(\frac Xn\right).
0321 | \]
0322 | \end{lemma}
0323 | \dokvo
0324 | \[
0325 | \Delta(X)=\psi(X)-\flr{X}=\sum_{m\le X}(\log-d)*\mu(m)=\sum_{m\le X}\sum_{n\mid m}(\log n-d(n))\mu\left(\frac mn\right)
0326 | =\sum_{n\le X}(\log n-d(n))\sum_{h\le\frac Xn}\mu(h).
0327 | \]
0328 | 
0329 | The following lemma is a consequence of Lemma~\ref{PreobMertensLem}
0330 | and the inversion formula (Theorem~\ref{PreobInversionF}).
0331 | \begin{lemma}\label{PreobMertensfromDelta}
0332 | We have
0333 | \[
0334 | M(X)=\sum_{n\le X}b_n\Delta\left(\frac Xn\right),
0335 | \]
0336 | where
0337 | \[
0338 | b_n=\begin{cases}
0339 | -1&\text{if $n=1$},\\
0340 | (-1)\left(\log n-d(n)+\sum\limits_{\substack{n_1n_2=n\\ n_1,n_2\not\in\{1,n\}}}(\log n_1-d(n_1))
0341 | (\log n_2-d(n_2))\right.&\\
0342 | \left.+\sum\limits_{\substack{n_1n_2n_3=n\\ n_1,n_2,n_3\not\in\{1,n\}}}(\log n_1-d(n_1))
0343 | (\log n_2-d(n_2))(\log n_3-d(n_3))+\cdots\right)&\text{if $n>1$}.
0344 | \end{cases}
0345 | \]
0346 | \end{lemma}
0347 | 
0348 | Let $X=6$.
0349 | Then we have:
0350 | \begin{alignat*}{2}
0351 | \Delta_{(1)}(X) &= \psi(X)-\flr{X}=2\log2+\log3+\log5-6, &\qquad M_{(1)}(X) &= M(X)=-1,\\
0352 | \Delta_{(2)}(X) &= \psi\left(\frac X2\right)-\flr{\frac X2}=\log2+\log3-3, & M_{(2)}(X) &= M\left(\frac X2\right)=-1,\\
0353 | \Delta_{(3)}(X) &= \psi\left(\frac X3\right)-\flr{\frac X3}=\log2-2, & M_{(3)}(X) &= M\left(\frac X3\right)=0,\\
0354 | \Delta_{(4)}(X) &= \psi\left(\frac X4\right)-\flr{\frac X4}=-1, & M_{(4)}(X) &= M\left(\frac X4\right)=1,\\
0355 | \Delta_{(5)}(X) &= \psi\left(\frac X5\right)-\flr{\frac X5}=-1, & M_{(5)}(X) &= M\left(\frac X5\right)=1,\\
0356 | 
0357 | \Delta_{(\flr{X})}(X) &= \psi\left(\frac X{\flr{X}}\right)-\flr{\frac X{\flr{X}}}=-1, & M_{(\flr{X})}(X) &= M\left(\frac X{\flr{X}}\right)=1.
0358 | \end{alignat*}
0359 | By Lemma~\ref{PreobMertensLem}, we can set up the nonsingular system of simultaneous linear equations
0360 | with the upper triangular sparse matrix:
0361 | \begin{equation*}
0362 | \begin{pmatrix}
0363 | \Delta_{(1)} \\
0364 | \Delta_{(2)} \\
0365 | \Delta_{(3)} \\
0366 | \Delta_{(4)} \\
0367 | \Delta_{(5)} \\
0368 | \Delta_{(6)}
0369 | \end{pmatrix}
0370 | =
0371 | \begin{pmatrix}
0372 | -1 & \log2-2 & \log3-2 & 2\log2-3 & \log5-2 & \log2+\log3-4 \\
0373 | 0 & -1 & 0 & \log2-2 & 0 & \log3-2 \\
0374 | 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 & 0 & \log2-2 \\
0375 | 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\
0376 | 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\
0377 | 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1
0378 | \end{pmatrix}
0379 | \begin{pmatrix}
0380 | M_{(1)} \\
0381 | M_{(2)} \\
0382 | M_{(3)} \\
0383 | M_{(4)} \\
0384 | M_{(5)} \\
0385 | M_{(6)}
0386 | \end{pmatrix}.
0387 | \end{equation*}
0388 | Solving the system by Cramer's rule, as in the proof (see below) of the inversion formula (Theorem~\ref{PreobInversionF}),
0389 | we obtain
0390 | \footnotesize
0391 | \begin{equation*}
0392 | \begin{split}
0393 | &M_{(1)}(X)=M(X)=\\
0394 | &\begin{pmatrix}
0395 | -1, & 2-\log2, & 2-\log3, & -(\log2)^2+2\log2-1, & 2-\log5, & -2\log2\log3+3\log2+3\log3-4
0396 | \end{pmatrix}
0397 | \begin{pmatrix}
0398 | \Delta_{(1)} \\
0399 | \Delta_{(2)} \\
0400 | \Delta_{(3)} \\
0401 | \Delta_{(4)} \\
0402 | \Delta_{(5)} \\
0403 | \Delta_{(6)}
0404 | \end{pmatrix},
0405 | \end{split}
0406 | \end{equation*}
0407 | \normalsize
0408 | which coincides with the assertion of Lemma~\ref{PreobMertensfromDelta}.
0409 | 
0410 | \textbf{3. Proof of Inversion formula.}
0411 | \begin{theorem}[Inversion Formula] Let
0412 | \be\label{PreobFX}
0413 | F(X)=\sum_{n\le X}\alpha(n)G\left(\frac Xn\right).
0414 | \ee
0415 | Then we have
0416 | \[
0417 | G(X)=\sum_{n\le X}\beta(n)F\left(\frac Xn\right),
0418 | \]
0419 | where
0420 | \be\label{Preobbetanproof}
0421 | \beta(n)=\begin{cases}
0422 | \frac1{\alpha(1)}&\text{if $n=1$},\\
0423 | \frac1{\alpha(1)}&\left(-\frac{\alpha(n)}{\alpha(1)}+\sum\limits_{\substack{n_1n_2=n\\ n_1,n_2\not\in\{1,n\}}}\frac{\alpha(n_1)
0424 | \alpha(n_2)}{(-\alpha(1))^2}+\sum\limits_{\substack{n_1n_2n_3=n\\ n_1,n_2,n_3\not\in\{1,n\}}}\frac{\alpha(n_1)
0425 | \alpha(n_2)\alpha(n_3)}{(-\alpha(1))^3}+\cdots\right)\\
0426 | &\text{if $n>1$}.
0427 | \end{cases}
0428 | \ee
0429 | \end{theorem}
0430 | 
0431 | \dokvo
0432 | We use the following notation:
0433 | \begin{alignat*}{2}
0434 | F_{(1)}(X) &= F(X), &\qquad G_{(1)}(X) &= G(X),\\
0435 | F_{(2)}(X) &= F\left(\frac X2\right), & G_{(2)}(X) &= G\left(\frac X2\right),\\
0436 | &\cdots, & &\cdots,\\
0437 | F_{(\flr{X})}(X) &= F\left(\frac X{\flr{X}}\right), & G_{(\flr{X})}(X) &= G\left(\frac X{\flr{X}}\right).
0438 | \end{alignat*}
0439 | By~\eqref{PreobFX}, we can set up the nonsingular system of simultaneous linear equations
0440 | with the upper triangular sparse matrix $A$:
0441 | \[
0442 | \begin{split}
0443 | F_{(1)}(X)&=\sum_{1\le n\le X}\alpha(n)G_{(n)}(X),\\
0444 | F_{(2)}(X)&=\sum_{1\le n\le X/2}\alpha(n)G_{(2n)}(X),\\
0445 | &\cdots,\\
0446 | F_{(\flr{X})}(X)&=\sum_{1\le n\le X/\flr{X}}\alpha(n)G_{(\flr{X}n)}(X).
0447 | \end{split}
0448 | \]
0449 | Dividing every equation by $-\alpha(1)$ we obtain the new matrix $A'$ with the new entries $\alpha'(n)$.
0450 | By Cramer's rule,
0451 | \[
0452 | G_{(1)}(X)=G(X)=\sum_{n\le X}\beta(n)F\left(\frac Xn\right),
0453 | \]
0454 | where
0455 | \[
0456 | \beta(n)=\frac{(-1)^{n+1}\det{A'}_{n,1}}{(-\alpha(1))\det A'}.
0457 | \]
0458 | For $n\ge3$ we multiply $i$-th row $\overline{r}_i$, starting from $i=2$, of matrix ${A'}_{n,1}$
0459 | by
0460 | \[
0461 | S_i=\left(\alpha'(i)+\sum_{\substack{n_1n_2=i\\ n_1,n_2\not\in\{1,i\}}}\alpha'(n_1)
0462 | \alpha'(n_2)+\sum_{\substack{n_1n_2n_3=i\\ n_1,n_2,n_3\not\in\{1,i\}}}\alpha'(n_1)
0463 | \alpha'(n_2)\alpha'(n_3)+\cdots\right),
0464 | \]
0465 | and make the assignment $\overline{r}_i\leftarrow S_i\overline{r}_i+\overline{r}_{i-1}$ (for $2\le i\le(n-1)$)
0466 | to transform ${A'}_{n,1}$ to an upper triangular matrix.
0467 | This yields formula~\eqref{Preobbetanproof} for $\beta(n)$.
0468 | 
0469 | \textbf{4. Proof of Theorem~\ref{PreobZZ}.}
0470 | 
0471 | Consider the case of $\chi$ an even character,
0472 | that is, $\chi(-1)=1$.
0473 | Following Pintz~\cite{PreobPintz2},
0474 | define the entire function
0475 | \[
0476 | g_{\chi}(s):=\frac{L(s-1,\chi)}{(s-1-\beta_0)\prod_{\nu=1}^2(s-1+2\nu)},
0477 | \]
0478 | and let
0479 | \[
0480 | \lambda:=\log X-2,
0481 | \]
0482 | \[
0483 | r_{\lambda}(H):=\frac1{2\pi i}\inte_{(3)}e^{s^2/\lambda+Hs}g_{\chi}(s)\,ds.
0484 | \]
0485 | Using formula
0486 | \[
0487 | \inte_{1}^{\infty}\frac{M_{\chi}(x,y_0)}{x^s}dx=\frac{1}{(s-1)L(s-1,\chi)}\prod_{3\le p\le y_0}
0488 | \left(1-\frac{\chi(p)}{p^{s-1}}\right)^{-1},
0489 | \]
0490 | where $\Re s=\sigma>2$ and $y_0\asymp\exp\left(c(\log X)^{2/5}(\log_{(2)}X)^{1/5}\right)$,
0491 | and interchanging the integrals, we get
0492 | \[
0493 | \begin{split}
0494 | U&\mathrel{{:}{=}}\inte_1^{\infty}M_{\chi}(x,y_0)r_{\lambda}(\lambda-\log x)dx\\
0495 | &=\frac1{2\pi i}\inte_{(3)}e^{s^2/\lambda+\lambda s}g_{\chi}(s)
0496 | \inte_1^{\infty}\frac{M_{\chi}(x,y_0)}{x^{s}}\,dx\,ds\\
0497 | &=\frac1{2\pi i}\inte_{(3)}e^{s^2/\lambda+\lambda s}
0498 | \frac{\prod_{3\le p\le y_0}
0499 | \left(1-\frac{\chi(p)}{p^{s-1}}\right)^{-1}}{(s-1-\beta_0)(s-1)\prod_{\nu=1}^2(s-1+2\nu)}\,ds.
0500 | \end{split}
0501 | \]
0502 | Thus,
0503 | \[
0504 | \begin{split}
0505 | U&=\mathop{\text{\textup Res}}_{s=1+\beta_0}e^{s^2/\lambda+\lambda s}
0506 | \frac{\prod_{3\le p\le y_0}
0507 | \left(1-\frac{\chi(p)}{p^{s-1}}\right)^{-1}}{(s-1-\beta_0)(s-1)\prod_{\nu=1}^2(s-1+2\nu)}
0508 | +O\left(X^{1+\beta_0-1/\log y_0}\log y_0\right)\\
0509 | &=\frac{e^{(1+\beta_0)^2/\lambda+(1+\beta_0)\lambda}
0510 | \prod_{3\le p\le y_0}
0511 | \left(1-\frac{\chi(p)}{p^{\beta_0}}\right)^{-1}}{\beta_0\prod_{\nu=1}^2(\beta_0+2\nu)}
0512 | +O\left(X^{1+\beta_0-1/\log y_0}\log y_0\right)\\
0513 | &\gg\frac{X^{1+\beta_0}}{\log y_0}.
0514 | \end{split}
0515 | \]
0516 | Now we derive an upper bound for $|U|$.
0517 | First, if $H\le-2$ ($H=\lambda-\log x=\log X-\log x-2$), we integrate along the line $\sigma=\lambda$ instead of $\sigma=3$:
0518 | \[
0519 | |r_{\lambda}(H)|\le\frac1{2\pi}\inte_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{\lambda-t^2/\lambda-|H|\lambda}
0520 | \frac2{\lambda-2}\,dt\le e^{-\lambda(|H|-1)},
0521 | \]
0522 | and by the trivial estimate $M_{\chi}(x,y_0)\le x$ we have
0523 | for the part of the integral with $x\ge X$:
0524 | \[
0525 | \begin{split}
0526 | &\left|\inte_X^{\infty}M_{\chi}(x,y_0)r_{\lambda}(\lambda-\log x)dx\right|
0527 | \le\inte_{e^{\lambda+2}}^{\infty}xe^{-\lambda(\log x-\lambda-1)}\,dx\\
0528 | =&\left.\frac{e^{\lambda^2+\lambda}x^{2-\lambda}}{2-\lambda}\right|_{x=e^{\lambda+2}}^{x=+\infty}
0529 | =\frac{e^{\lambda+4}}{\lambda-2}\ll X.
0530 | \end{split}
0531 | \]
0532 | Next, we move the line of integration in $r_{\lambda}(H)$ to $\sigma=0$.
0533 | By the functional equation for Dirichlet $L$-functions and the Stirling formula we get
0534 | \[
0535 | L(-1+it,\chi)\ll q^{3/2}|t|^{3/2},
0536 | \]
0537 | hence for an arbitrary $H$
0538 | \[
0539 | |r_{\lambda}(H)|\ll\inte_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{q^{3/2}|t|^{3/2}}{|t|^3}\,dt\ll q^{3/2},
0540 | \]
0541 | so
0542 | \[
0543 | |U|\ll q^{3/2}\inte_1^X|M_{\chi}(x,y_0)|\,dx.
0544 | \]
0545 | Combining the upper and the lower estimates, we obtain
0546 | \[
0547 | \frac{X^{1+\beta_0}}{q^{3/2}\log y_0}\ll
0548 | \inte_1^X|M_{\chi}(x,y_0)|\,dx.
0549 | \]
0550 | 
0551 | By an argument similar to that of Koukoulopoulos~\cite{PreobKoukoulo},
0552 | denoting by $c$ a certain positive constant, not necessarily the same one in every place,
0553 | for $y_0\asymp\exp\left(c(\log X)^{2/5}(\log_{(2)}X)^{1/5}\right)$,
0554 | $q\asymp\exp\left(c(\log X)^{2/5}(\log_{(2)}X)^{1/5}\right)$
0555 | and $X^c\ll x\ll X$
0556 | we have
0557 | \[
0558 | |M_{\chi}(x,y_0)|\ll xe^{-c(\log x)^{3/5}(\log_{(2)}x)^{-1/5}}.
0559 | \]
0560 | Thus,
0561 | \[
0562 | \beta_0\le1-\frac{c}{\log q}
0563 | \]
0564 | and the constant $c>0$ is effectively computable.
